title: Earning the Right to Break the Rules
text:
In 1958 the social psychologist Edwin Hollander tried to solve a puzzle. Groups expect their members to conform, yet they also expect their leaders to bring change, which means breaking with what the group has always done. How do leaders get away with it?

Hollander proposed that each member of a group builds up a kind of account in the eyes of the others, which he called idiosyncrasy credit. Credit is earned by showing competence on the group's task and by conforming to its norms, showing that one is loyal and shares its values. Members who have built up enough credit gain status, and with it the freedom to deviate and to propose new directions. Members who deviate before they have earned that credit are seen as troublemakers and lose influence.

Hollander then tested the idea in experiments with small groups solving a series of problems. A planted group member who gave good answers and followed the group's agreed procedures early on, and only later challenged them, ended up with far more influence than one who challenged the group's procedures from the start, even when both were equally competent.
lesson: A new leader who changes everything on day one meets resistance. First show competence and respect for the group, and you earn the trust to lead it somewhere new.
source: Hollander, E. P. (1958). Conformity, status, and idiosyncrasy credit. Psychological Review, 65(2), 117-127.
caveat: The 1958 paper was theoretical; the supporting experiments came in Hollander's later work, notably in 1960.
